input:
When the speed of a centrifugal pump is changed, its flow, its head, and the power it draws all change along with it, and the relationships which govern these changes are collectively known as the affinity laws. In what follows, the three proportionalities comprising the laws are set out and a worked check is then presented, in which it is shown that doubling the speed has the striking consequence of multiplying the power by 8.

It should be borne in mind throughout that the affinity laws pertain to one particular pump, in an unchanged condition and handling one particular liquid. The first of the laws states that the flow is proportional to the speed, so that at twice the speed the pump may be expected to deliver twice the flow. According to the second law, the head is proportional to the square of the speed, whilst according to the third law, the power is proportional to the cube of the speed. It must be emphasised that the laws serve to compare points on the characteristic of one and the same pump, and that they tell us nothing whatsoever about a different pump; furthermore, they presuppose that the efficiency at the two speeds under consideration remains near enough unchanged, an assumption which is generally satisfied for speed changes of the magnitude effected in service by a variable-speed drive.

By way of a worked check, let it be supposed that the speed rises by a factor of 2. The flow then rises by the factor 2 itself. The head, for its part, rises by the factor 2 squared, which works out to 4. The power, meanwhile, rises by the factor 2 cubed, which works out to 8. The cube appearing in the power law is thus the term which effectively governs the loading of the motor: the power at the raised speed is fully 8 times the power at the original speed, and a motor which was selected with little margin at the original speed will find itself overloaded at the raised speed, notwithstanding that the flow has done no more than double.
target:
A centrifugal pump run at a new speed delivers a new flow, a new head, and a new power, and the affinity laws give all three changes from the speed change alone. This passage states the three proportionalities and works one check in full: doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8.

The affinity laws apply to one pump, unchanged, handling the one liquid. The flow is proportional to the speed: at twice the speed, the pump delivers twice the flow. The head is proportional to the square of the speed. The power is proportional to the cube of the speed. The laws compare points on the characteristic of the one pump; they state nothing about a different pump, and they hold where the efficiency at the two speeds is near enough unchanged, which is the case for speed changes of the size a variable-speed drive makes in service.

The laws are used in both directions. Run forward, they give the duty a pump delivers when its speed is raised to meet a higher demand, before any drive is ordered or fitted. Run backward, they give the duty surrendered when the speed is cut, and the cube in the power law is what makes the cut worth making: on a duty where the flow is held down by throttling, a speed reduction removes the throttling loss and reduces the power by the cube of the speed ratio at the same time.

Worked check: let the speed rise by a factor of 2. The flow rises by the factor 2 itself. The head rises by the factor 2 squared, which is 4. The power rises by the factor 2 cubed, which is 8. The cube in the power law is the term that governs motor loading: the power at the raised speed is 8 times the power at the original speed, and a motor chosen with little margin at the original speed is overloaded at the raised speed even though the flow has only doubled.
